title: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE TOLD PETER TO FORGIVE “SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN”
paragraphs: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE TOLD PETER TO FORGIVE “SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN”
Peter wanted to know when forgiveness could finally stop. Jesus answered with a number—but He was really exposing something buried much deeper in the human heart.
There is probably a name you do not like remembering.
Maybe you have forgiven them.
At least, you said you did.
But then somebody mentions their name.
Your chest tightens.
The conversation starts replaying.
The betrayal comes back in color.
The words return with their original sharpness.
And suddenly you realize something uncomfortable:
The event happened years ago...
but part of you is still standing in the room where they hurt you.
That is why one question Peter asked Jesus nearly two thousand years ago still feels painfully modern.
Peter came to Jesus and asked:
“Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Then Jesus answered him.
The Greek of Matthew 18:22 reads:
“Οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις, ἀλλὰ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά.”
Ou legō soi heōs heptakis, alla heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.
In straightforward terms:
“I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

Some translations render the final expression “seventy-seven times.” The Greek phrase, ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά — hebdomēkontakis hepta, has generated discussion over precisely which numerical rendering is best.
But do not miss Jesus while arguing over the arithmetic.
Whether you understand the expression as seventy-seven or seventy times seven, Jesus was not handing Peter a forgiveness calculator.
He was destroying the calculator.
Peter wanted a number.
Jesus confronted the heart that wanted to count.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes ours.
Because we count too.
We remember the first lie.
The second betrayal.
The third apology that changed nothing.
The fourth promise they broke.
We remember what they posted.
What they whispered.
What they stole.
What they did to the marriage.
What they did to the family.
What they did to our reputation.
What they did when nobody else was watching.
We count because counting gives pain a structure.
And sometimes keeping the record makes us feel safer.
“If I remember exactly what you did, maybe you will never have the opportunity to destroy me again.”
That feeling is understandable.
But Jesus was showing Peter that there is a difference between wisdom and vengeance, between remembering what happened and making someone’s debt the center of your life.
Peter’s question was essentially:
“Jesus, when have I forgiven enough?”
And Jesus’ answer was essentially:
“Peter, you still think forgiveness is something you measure.”
Then Jesus told a story.
And this is where the passage becomes devastating.
A king decided to settle accounts with his servants.
One servant was brought before him owing an enormous debt.
The amount Jesus names is ten thousand talents.
It is difficult to translate that ancient amount neatly into modern money, and perhaps that is precisely why we should resist reducing it to a sensational dollar figure.
The point is simpler and more frightening.
The debt was impossibly large for the servant to repay.
He was finished.
There was no clever financial plan coming.
No second job.
No hidden savings account.
No way out.
He fell before the king and pleaded for patience.
And then something happened he had no right to expect.
The master had compassion on him.
He released him.
And forgave the debt.
Imagine walking into a room carrying a debt you could never repay...
and walking out owing nothing.
That is grace.
But Jesus was not finished.
The forgiven servant walked outside and found another servant who owed him a comparatively tiny amount.
And suddenly the man who had just received mercy became merciless.
He grabbed the other servant.
He demanded payment.
The other man pleaded with language strikingly similar to the plea he himself had just made.
But he refused.
Think about that.
The hands that had just received mercy were now wrapped around somebody else’s throat.
And before condemning him too quickly, look carefully into the mirror.
How many times have we walked out of worship celebrating the forgiveness of God...
and then gone home refusing to forgive someone else?
We sing about grace.
We post verses about grace.
We thank Jesus for grace.
We tell people we are saved by grace.
But then somebody actually needs grace from us.
Suddenly...
we become accountants.
That is the scandal Jesus exposes.
The servant had forgotten the size of the debt from which he had been released.
And perhaps unforgiveness often grows in the same soil.
We remember what they owe us while slowly forgetting what Christ forgave in us.
That does not mean what happened to you was insignificant.
Christian forgiveness does not require calling evil good.
It does not mean abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean betrayal did not matter.
It does not mean justice suddenly becomes sinful.
It does not mean you must immediately restore trust to an unrepentant person.
It does not mean reconciliation can always happen instantly—or even safely.
Forgiveness and trust are not identical.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Reconciliation ordinarily involves more than one heart. Forgiveness is the refusal to make personal vengeance, hatred, and endless debt-collection the throne of your own heart.
Jesus never commands you to pretend darkness is light.
He commands something far more supernatural.
Bring the debt to God.
Release your personal claim to vengeance.
Refuse to let another person’s sin turn you into a prisoner of hatred.
And keep doing it when the memory returns.
Sometimes forgiveness happens in a moment.
Sometimes the decision happens in a moment and the emotional healing takes much longer.
You may forgive someone today and wake tomorrow with the wound screaming again.
That does not necessarily mean yesterday’s forgiveness was fake.
It may mean the wound still needs healing.
And perhaps “seventy times seven” becomes painfully real there.
Not merely forgiving seventy different offenses...
but bringing the same wound back to Jesus whenever bitterness tries to resurrect it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
“Jesus, I gave this to You yesterday.”
Give it to Him again.
“Jesus, I thought I had forgiven them.”
Bring the pain back again.
“Jesus, why does remembering still hurt?”
Tell Him the truth again.
Forgiveness is not pretending you no longer bleed.
Sometimes forgiveness means refusing to use the blood as ink to write the rest of your life.
And there may be an even deeper biblical echo behind Jesus’ words.
Long before Peter asked his question, Genesis recorded the chilling boast of Lamech.
Lamech spoke of vengeance multiplied far beyond Cain’s.
Genesis 4:24 speaks of vengeance “seventy-sevenfold” in common modern renderings.
Then generations later, Jesus speaks about forgiveness using strikingly similar numerical language.
The contrast is breathtaking.
Humanity says:
Multiply revenge.
Jesus says:
Multiply mercy.
Lamech represents the ancient instinct of fallen humanity:
“You hurt me, so I will hurt you worse.”
Jesus announces the kingdom:
“You have received mercy you could never purchase, so do not build your life around making others pay.”
That is not weakness.
Look at the cross before calling forgiveness weak.
Jesus was mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Nailed to wood.
And while human beings were committing an unspeakable injustice against Him, Luke records Him praying:
“Father, forgive them.”
The cross is where Christianity destroys our illusion that forgiveness means sin does not matter.
If sin did not matter, there would be no cross.
At Calvary we discover both realities simultaneously:
Sin is more serious than we wanted to believe.
Grace is more magnificent than we dared to imagine.
God did not save us by pretending our debt did not exist.
Christ bore sin.
Jesus entered our judgment.
The innocent Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And because of His death and resurrection, forgiveness is offered not as a reward for people who finally become respectable, but as grace received through repentance and faith in Christ.
This is why the Gospel is scandalous.
The adulterer can be forgiven.
The liar can be forgiven.
The addict can be forgiven.
The hypocrite can be forgiven.
The religious fraud can be forgiven.
The person carrying secret shame can be forgiven.
The person everybody else has written off can be forgiven.
Even you.
Even me.
Not because our sins were small.
Because Jesus is enough.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding for years.
You have been asking God to forgive you while secretly believing your particular sin sits outside the reach of the cross.
You know the verse.
You know the sermon.
You know the theology.
But when the lights go out and the room becomes quiet, shame whispers:
“Not you.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say your sin was nothing.
The Gospel says Christ is greater.
Repentance is not pretending you never fell.
Repentance turns from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace changes what the scandal gets to become.
Peter himself would eventually understand this in a way he probably could not have imagined when he asked about forgiveness.
This was Peter.
The outspoken disciple.
The man who promised loyalty.
The man who insisted that even if others fell away, he would remain.
And then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
Denial.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster.
Imagine that sound.
Imagine realizing that the mouth which had confessed Jesus as the Christ had just denied knowing Him.
Peter did not merely witness somebody else’s scandal.
Peter became the scandal.
Yet Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
The failure was real.
The denial was real.
The tears were real.
But failure did not receive the final sentence.
Grace did.
That is our theme because that is the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing the need for repentance.
But by taking repentant sinners whose stories looked finished and making their lives testimonies of redeeming grace.
Peter asked how many times he needed to forgive someone else.
One day Peter would discover how desperately he himself needed forgiveness.
Maybe that is why this passage refuses to leave us comfortable.
Because eventually every one of us occupies both sides of the story.
We have been wounded.
And we have wounded others.
We have been lied to.
And we have lied.
We have needed mercy.
And we have withheld mercy.
We have been the person crying because somebody broke our heart.
And somewhere in our history, somebody may have cried because of us.
The Gospel leaves no room for superiority at the foot of the cross.
There are only sinners who need a Savior.
So think about that name again.
The person you thought of at the beginning.
Maybe forgiving them feels impossible.
Do not confuse forgiveness with pretending nothing happened.
Bring what happened into the light.
Seek wise help when necessary.
Maintain appropriate boundaries where necessary.
Pursue justice through rightful means where necessary.
But do not surrender your soul to bitterness.
You have already given that person enough.
Do not give them your future too.
And perhaps the person you cannot forgive is yourself.
You keep replaying the worst thing you ever did as though endless self-punishment could somehow improve upon the sacrifice of Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Confess honestly.
Turn away from sin.
But if you belong to Christ, stop treating shame like a second savior.
Shame cannot atone for you.
Jesus already shed the blood.
There is only one Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need proof that healing does not require hatred.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not somebody you want to attack with an article.
Somebody who is tired.
Somebody whose heart has become heavy from carrying what another person did.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when an old wound knocks again.
You may need to remember that forgiveness is not saying, “What happened did not matter.”
It is saying, “What happened will not become my master. Jesus is my Lord.”
It does not. The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God in Christ.
But generosity can be one practical way believers choose to help truthful, Christ-centered teaching reach more people.
But before you leave...
remember Peter’s question.
“How many times?”
We still ask it.
How many times must I forgive?
How many times must I surrender this memory?
How many times must I refuse bitterness?
How many times must I bring this wound back to Jesus?
And Christ keeps pulling our eyes away from the calculator...
and toward the cross.
Because forgiven people were never meant to spend their lives counting everybody else’s debts.
Maybe tonight the miracle is not that you finally forget what happened.
Maybe the miracle begins when what happened finally stops owning you.
The wound may explain part of your story—but because of Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
